key_insights: Asia saw a partial semiconductor rebound after last week's selloff, fading through the session: TSMC +4.6%, MediaTek +9.8%, Tokyo Electron +2.7%, Advantest +1.29%, Taiex +4.9%, Nikkei +2.3%, Kospi -80bps. Taiwan's tighter short selling rules and NT$500bn stabilization fund are providing support.

NDX futures would probably be considerably higher without the weekend Nvidia/Jensen Huang headlines. The author reads them as idiosyncratic rather than a broader AI read-through, but they could affect sentiment. CoreWeave (Tuesday) and Nebius (Thursday) earnings matter more for underlying AI sentiment.
Last week saw the largest cut in US long/short TMT gross since Covid and the biggest cut in net since Liberation day. Almost everything linked to AI spending was sold.

The post mid-term rally lasted 24 hours. Short covering was followed by the realization that one cannot be this pessimistic on AI spending and this optimistic on the broader economy. The SPX moved outside its recent range, gamma support disappeared, CTA selling accelerated, and double digit semiconductor declines compounded the deleveraging.
Models suggest roughly another $25bn+ of SPX CTA supply this week.

CPI on Tuesday is the main macro event. Friday's payrolls were strong (+165k, wages +0.4% MoM, unemployment 4.1%), adding pressure on the Fed, though political uncertainty and AI concerns currently dominate. Treasury auctions: 3yr Monday, 10yr Tuesday, 30yr Thursday.
Congress returns for its lame duck session. A bipartisan energy permitting bill is potentially positive for data centers, but passage is uncertain.

Oil is lower to start the week with no weekend escalation in Iran. Messaging was conflicting: Trump suggested further strikes are unlikely if negotiations progress, Rubio said talks have been largely unproductive. The USS Theodore Roosevelt is not expected in the region before mid-November. Absent diplomatic progress, the author expects the escalation premium to return to oil by Wednesday/Thursday ahead of the weekend.
Russia/Ukraine: trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi November 10-11, with prediction markets assigning 10-15% odds of a year-end ceasefire. The author's base case is a prolonged conflict.

Defense has derated sharply. US top-line defense spending could be maintained in a lame duck compromise with Democrats on healthcare. European defense is asymmetric: ceasefire headlines and EU fiscal debates drove multiple compression, but NATO 2%+ GDP commitments and multi-year order backlogs mean much bad news is already priced in.

The author does not accept the long-term bear argument that power constraints, permits and political delays undermine the AI buildout. If demand is real, capacity migrates to other states, countries or alternative power sources. Example: Mississippi is defending xAI's 2GW Southaven buildout in federal court and secured over $25 billion in AWS commitments.

Oversupply, not power or permitting, is the key medium-term AI risk. GPU spot rental rates remain supported by scarcity, but optimization and smaller specialized models are compressing per-token inference costs. The bear argument is now that efficiency gains could outpace demand growth.

Semis look oversold, and the author would move up the quality curve first (ASML, TSMC). The Friday bounce was inevitable, and whether to buy or sell it depends on incoming evidence on demand and monetization.

The macro backdrop has improved (energy lower, rates retracing, credit spreads tightening). Nasdaq has broken below its 200-day, making a dip-buying backtest harder, while the S&P's broader trend remains intact. CTA supply and retail selling are headwinds, with CPI the immediate catalyst. The best outcome is range-bound trading, letting implied volatility compress and systematic demand rebuild.
